Surely
shŭr'lŭ
adv. (certainly, without fail; in the Authorized Version the marker of a divine oath, and the first word the serpent contradicted)
From sure (Old French sur, from Latin securus, free from care) plus -ly. In the Old Testament it very often renders not an adverb at all but a Hebrew emphatic construction — the infinitive doubled with its own verb, which English can only carry by adding a word.

Biblical Definition

Surely is the Authorized Version's way of rendering a Hebrew emphasis that has no English equivalent: the verb is written twice, once as an infinitive and once as a finite form, and the effect is to place the whole weight of the speaker behind the statement. Hence the first threat in Scripture: “in the day that thou eatest thereof thou shalt surely die” (Gen 2:17) — literally dying thou shalt die. And hence the first lie in Scripture is built by inserting one word into it: “Ye shall not surely die” (Gen 3:4). The serpent does not deny God's existence or His authorship of the command; he denies the certainty of the sanction, and every temptation since has been assembled the same way. Elsewhere the word marks the oath of judgment — “Surely none of the men that came up out of Egypt… shall see the land” (Num 32:11) — and the oath of grace, which is where Scripture ends: “Surely I come quickly” (Rev 22:20). Jacob's waking at Bethel gives the word its most human use: “Surely the LORD is in this place; and I knew it not” (Gen 28:16).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines surely as certainly, undoubtedly, without doubt — and notes its use to affirm a thing firmly, as in the divine asseverations of Scripture.

expand to see more

SURELY, adv. Certainly; undoubtedly; firmly.

He that createth all things, surely he is God.

2. Firmly; without danger of falling. He that walketh uprightly, walketh surely. Prov. x.

Note. In the Scriptures it frequently renders the Hebrew idiom in which the verb is doubled for emphasis, as, dying thou shalt die.

Key Scripture

Gen 2:17 — "But of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, thou shalt not eat of it: for in the day that thou eatest thereof thou shalt surely die."

Gen 3:4 — "And the serpent said unto the woman, Ye shall not surely die:"

Num 32:11 — "Surely none of the men that came up out of Egypt, from twenty years old and upward, shall see the land which I sware unto Abraham, unto Isaac, and unto Jacob; because they have not wholly followed me:"

Gen 28:16 — "And Jacob awaked out of his sleep, and he said, Surely the LORD is in this place; and I knew it not."

Modern Corruption

The oldest attack on Scripture is not the denial of God but the softening of His sanction — and it is still made by adding a single qualifying word to a plain threat.

expand to see more

Gen 3:4 is the model of every subsequent corruption of the word of God, and its method is worth naming exactly. The serpent grants the command, grants the Commander, and negates only the certainty: ye shall not surely die. He follows it with a motive — God is withholding something good — and the woman, who had already added a clause of her own to the prohibition, acts. Nothing in the exchange is crude. It is a hermeneutic, and it is the same one at work wherever hell is quietly reduced to a metaphor, wherever a plain command is called culturally conditioned, wherever the certainty of judgment becomes a possibility to be weighed.

The remedy is not to shout the threats but to notice that God binds Himself with the same word. Surely is the vocabulary of the divine oath, and Heb 6:17-18 says why God swears at all: to show the heirs of promise the immutability of His counsel, so that by two immutable things the believer might have strong consolation. The same certainty that makes Gen 2:17 terrible makes Rev 22:20 sweet. A God whose threats can be softened has promises that can be softened too, and the man who talks himself out of the first has lost the second in the same breath.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

English sure from Latin securus; rendering the Hebrew infinitive absolute construction (verb doubled for emphasis) and Greek particles of asseveration such as nai and men.

expand to see more

Hebrew infinitive absolute — the verb written twice, as moth tamuth (Gen 2:17), literally “dying thou shalt die”; the KJV renders the doubling with surely.

Gen 3:4 in Hebrew — lo moth temuthun, the same doubled construction with a negative laid across it; the serpent quotes the grammar and reverses the verdict.

Hebrew aken (H403) — surely, truly; Jacob's word at Bethel, “Surely the LORD is in this place” (Gen 28:16).

Hebrew im in oath formulas — “Surely none of the men…” (Num 32:11) is an elliptical oath: if they shall see the land, with the curse left unspoken.

Greek nai (G3483) — yea, surely; nai, erchomai tachu, “Surely I come quickly” (Rev 22:20).

Usage

"“Thou shalt surely die” — the Hebrew doubling, the whole weight of God behind a sanction."

"“Ye shall not surely die” — the first lie, made by qualifying a certainty."

"“Surely I come quickly” — the same oath-word, turned toward comfort."
